Field observations of the White-browed babbler (Pomatostomus superciliosus) reveal that freshly laid eggs incubated at 33 °C [T = 33 °C] require an average of 19.5 days [ab = 19.5 days] before hatching occurs, a developmental duration consistent with other cooperatively breeding Australo-Papuan passerines. The altricial nestlings emerge at a remarkably modest size, with the wet weight at birth recorded as 3.58 grams [Ww0 = 3.58 grams], reflecting the high degree of parental investment required throughout the nestling phase. During the post-hatching period, chicks are brooded intensively by all group members, leading to rapid initial growth. The age at fledging, marking the achievement of first sustained flight, occurs relatively quickly at 16.5 days after hatching [tx = 16.5 days after hatching], although some variation within the 19 to 20 day range has been noted in less productive seasons at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This developmental pace is somewhat faster than that observed in congeneric species occupying more temperate regions, possibly as an adaptation to the unpredictable rainfall patterns of the semi-arid and mallee zones they inhabit across southern Australia.

A captive study conducted under controlled thermal conditions provides detailed insight into the species' metabolic physiology. When maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which approximates the upper range of summer roost microclimates, adult White-browed babblers exhibited a basal metabolic rate of 61.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 61.8 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This mass-specific oxygen consumption is within the expected range for a passerine of its body size and aligns well with data from other cooperative breeders that face similar thermal challenges. The same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] was used to assess several key life-history transitions in the captive population. Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal development and reproductive hormone activation, was reached at 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching], indicating a relatively rapid physiological maturation compared to the timeline required for successful group integration and territory acquisition in the wild at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].

Body mass dimorphism is evident between the sexes of the White-browed babbler, with adult males attaining a larger asymptotic body size than females. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the maximum recorded adult body mass, stabilizes at 42 grams [Wwi = 42 grams], a figure that reflects the energetic constraints of egg production and incubation duties. In contrast, the ultimate wet weight for males reaches 44.4 grams [Wwi = 44.4 grams], a difference that may confer advantages in competitive interactions over breeding positions within the complex social hierarchy of this species. This sexual size divergence is not extreme but is consistent with partial reversed dimorphism seen in many Australian passerines, where females involved in prolonged brooding periods do not face the same energetic overhead as males engaged in territory defense and sentinel behavior. The body weights were derived from a large sample of wild-caught adults measured during the non-breeding season across multiple field sites in Victoria and South Australia, ensuring that the values represent fully grown individuals.

Reproductive output in the White-browed babbler is characterized by a conservative annual strategy typical of obligate cooperative breeders. Females lay between 1 and 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 1 and 6 eggs per clutch], with a single clutch produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch produced each year] under the thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that define the active metabolic season. This moderate clutch size, paired with extended helper-assisted provisioning, yields a modest overall annual reproductive rate. The first brood, representing the age at first successful breeding event, occurs at approximately 1.8 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.8 years after hatching], a delay that reflects the extended period young birds require to gain the social standing and experience necessary to either inherit a breeding position or disperse to found a new group at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This deferred reproduction is a hallmark of cooperative systems, where non-breeding helpers contribute to the survival of related offspring while waiting for breeding opportunities to arise in saturated habitats.

Longevity records for the White-browed babbler indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 5,256 days [am = approximately 5,256 days] from hatching, when measured under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic period. This comparatively extended lifespan for a small passerine is likely facilitated by the enhanced predator detection and sentinel behavior afforded by group living, which reduces the risk of mortality during vulnerable ages. The species' social system also buffers against food scarcity through cooperative foraging, allowing individuals to persist through drought years that would otherwise elevate mortality rates. When restated in terms of calendar years, the captive longevity record of 14.4 years [am = 14.4 years] places Pomatostomus superciliosus among the longer-lived members of its genus, a demographic trait that co-evolves with delayed first reproduction and low annual fecundity at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Senescence-related mortality in the wild likely occurs earlier, but banding recoveries have confirmed individuals exceeding twelve years of age in their natural habitat.
